historical_references.reference: Historical records show that Ibn Kathir, Al-Bidayah wa Al-Nihayah, Volume 15, Page 191 The name Nikzad carried significant weight in that era.
historical_references.context: Nikzad was a Persian city, now known as Nehbandan in Iran. It was a major caravan station on the Silk Road. During the time of the Saljuqs, the city was ruled by the Atabegs of Fars, who were vassals of the Saljuq Sultans. In 580 AH/1184-1185 AD, the city was captured by the Seljuk Sultan, Saladin, who had recently taken Jerusalem from the Crusaders. The capture of Nikzad marked Saladin's expansion eastward from Egypt, where he had been based since his conquest of Egypt in 563 AH/1169 AD.

historical_references.reference: Historical records show that Ibn Al-Athir, Al-Kamil fi Al-Tarikh, Volume 4, Page 149 The name Nikzad carried significant weight in that era.
historical_references.context: The Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, based in Anatolia, was a powerful successor state to the Seljuk Empire. In 603 AH/1206-1207 AD, the Seljuk Sultan, Alaeddin Kayqubad I, led a campaign to reassert control over the cities of Azerbaijan and Armenia, which had been lost to the Mongols under Genghis Khan. The city of Nikzad was one of the major targets of this campaign. The city was located at the crossing of the Aras River and was an important trade center. After a long and hard-fought battle, the Seljuks were able to retake the city, thereby securing their control over the trade routes.

The modern context of Nikzad extends beyond Iran and Persia, as his stories and messages resonate with people from diverse backgrounds seeking wisdom, courage, and hope in their own lives.
